“#Prevent, #Engage and#Act”

These were the three keywords I brought back home from the ReAct Asia Pacific Regional Conference on#AMR 2026, held in Jakarta last week.
 
Just ahead of#WAAW2026, clinicians, researchers, policymakers, CSOs and youth came together for two days to deliberate on a collective course of action for the years ahead.

#Prevent: The updated WHO Global Action Plan (2026–2036) puts prevention first. As one speaker put it, infection control, immunisation and WASH are among the most powerful AMR programmes we have. That means stopping infections before they need #antibiotics. Another session suggested teaching infection prevention to students early, so they carry it into practice and pass it on to their peers.

#Engage: AMR can’t be fixed by the health sector alone. One participant asked where the ministers of agriculture and environment were in the room, and another said the finance minister should be involved from day zero. The session that stayed with me most put people at the centre. AMR survivor Ankita Mitra reminded us that an infection may be diagnosed in one person, but the consequences are lived by an entire family. Civil society, communities, and young people have to be part of the solution.

#Act: Plans are only as good as their delivery. Most plans are not costed, and WHO shared that only about 10% of countries had domestic funding for their national action plans in 2024. The call from the room was to cost the plan, set measurable indicators, close the reporting gap, and scale what already works.

My biggest learning was seemingly obvious: AMR cannot be tackled without addressing the systemic challenges that sit beneath it. Plans stay unfunded, sectors stay siloed, and accountability stays weak. Access to antibiotics and diagnostics remains unequal, and infection control and primary care are still stretched thin. Climate change, disasters and conflict make all of this worse, because every flood or crisis can become an AMR event.
 
Underneath all of it is social inequity. Those who are poorer, more displaced, and further from care are the ones who face the weakest infection control, the limited access to diagnostics, and the highest costs when treatment fails. That is why so many well-designed plans don’t deliver: they work best for those who already have access. AMR is not only a health problem. It is a development problem and a health-system problem, and it needs to be treated as both.

We enountered some of these stories through the #SochSamajhKe fellowship, whichSuperheroes Against Superbugs organized earlier this year in collabortion withYouth Ki Awaaz. Seeing them echoed in Jakarta was a strong motivation for us to continue our work at SaS.

Sarsha Braim read her job offer on a bathroom break, halfway through a waitressing shift.

Last month she was in Cannes for MIPCOM (her first time in France), selling sport content to TV broadcasters alongside studios like Paramount and Disney.

Not long before that offer, she'd finished uni, applied for a few jobs in sport and heard nothing back. She had about 10 LinkedIn connections, all from one uni class, and was convinced that "I'm not some big CEO, so no one wants to hear from me."

55 days after joining TheSportsGrad Method, she was approached for a job at Inverleigh, a sports media company she'd never heard of.

So what did she do differently?

She started posting about ice hockey, a sport she genuinely loves and that hardly anyone in Australia was writing about. Then every time someone liked or reacted to a post, she sent them a connection request within 24 hours, "while it's still fresh," so they'd remember her name.

One of those people was a co-founder of Inverleigh. He passed her name on to the company's commercial director, and the director messaged her about a job.

Posting on LinkedIn gets you seen, but the job comes from what you do after someone notices you. Think of a like as a wave from across the street: you can wave back and keep walking, or you can cross the road and say hello.

Today Sarsha is Commercial Partnerships Manager, Asia Pacific, flying to Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia to sell sport content to broadcasters.

If you want to try it this week:
1. Pick a sport you could post about for months (bonus points if hardly anyone else is covering it).
2. Post one thing you've noticed about it through the lens of the job you want. Partnerships? Break down a club's sponsors. Events? Review a match day. Analytics? Unpack one stat.
3. Set a 24-hour rule: everyone who reacts gets a connection request with a short note about the post.

Devo, I know, most of your posts will get a handful of likes and plenty of people won't accept. But you're not waiting on a job ad anymore, and you only need the right person to remember you.

Congrats Sarsha!!

Representing Computer Science at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, our team (PriaIdaman) alongside Bintang Fajar Putra Pamungkas andMuhammad Rangga Nur Praditha developed INKLUSA, a Web-Based Decision Support System designed to empower regular teachers in inclusive classrooms.   

In many inclusive schools, teachers face high burnout due to limited special education support and time-consuming manual Individualized Education Programs (IEPs). Guided by the core philosophy that "a learning difficulty does not equal a lack of understanding," INKLUSA translates observable classroom barriers into actionable, evidence-based micro-interventions rooted in Universal Design for Learning (UDL).

Day 10 #UnEmployeeJourney #OpenToWork
My CV was rejected by a perfume brand. Not even invited for an interview, but it's ok :)

I have handled a local perfume brand before—from low awareness to shelf, from trial to repeat. And I have an obsession to build my own perfume brand. So I know the pain from the inside. 

What was in my head at that moment was this: "We need someone who can sell perfume in this crowded market".
My answer: "Everyone can sell perfume. Almost no one can make people REMEMBER perfume."

Look at their campaigns now: 15% - 35%++ discount in every campaign, and still low/not growing.

Discounts are not a strategy. It's a symptom.
A symptom that people try you once, and forget you tomorrow.

This is not a motivational post. This is my playbook.
👇 Day 10: #Perfume is Booming. But Everyone is#SellingPerfume.

THE DATA:
IDR 10,884 BILLION — Indonesia fragrance market 2025, 8.4% CAGR
USD 361M → USD 635M by 2035
9 out of 10 best-sellers on marketplace are LOCAL brands

Market is HUGE. Competition is BRUTAL.

WHY MOST BRANDS FAIL:
10 variants that all smell similar.
"Long-lasting 12 hours" + bottle photo + discount.
No hero. No story. No trial.
Result: Price war. No memory. No loyalty.

MY STRONG STRATEGY TO WIN:
1. SELL IDENTITY, NOT NOTES
Notes "vanilla, musk, amber."
But "For women who want to be remembered when they leave the room."

2. ONE HERO, NOT 10 COUSINS
1 HERO = 70% of budget, owns 1 persona
1 FIGHTER = for trial
1 LIMITED = for hype

3. SAMPLING IS YOUR MEDIA
Discovery Set 5 x 2ml + Full-Size Voucher.
Blind test on TikTok Live. Spray cards up to 500 micro-KOCs.
My KPI: 30% Discovery → Full Size in 14 days.
If not hit, your story is wrong, not your ad.

4. OWN TROPICAL + HALAL + LAYERING
Buyer asks in 5 seconds: Is it Halal? Will it last in Jakarta heat? Can I layer it?
Show 8-hour wear test + Halal cert upfront. Trust > Hype.

5. PROTECT YOUR HERO PRICE
Discovery Set = Entry. 30ml = Gift. 50ml = HERO, margin driver. 100ml = Premium.
Never discount the Hero. Discount the entry.

6. DIFFERENT JOBS PER CHANNEL, SAME PRICE
Marketplace & TikTok Shop = Trial
Beauty Store & Retail Store = Trust, Tester, Experience
Website = Loyalty, Refill, Member-Only

7. DROP, DON'T LAUNCH
500 pcs limited, numbered, early access.
Then let UGC sell: Scent Personality Quiz, Spray & React, and Rate My Perfume.

MY FORMULA:
Perfume = Trust x Memory x Trial

No Memory = Forgotten
No Trial = No Trust
No Trust = No Repeat

What is the ONE sentence people will remember about your perfume tomorrow?

If you don't have it yet, that's our first homework.

BI Rate +25 bps to 6,00% — A Pre-emptive Strike Against a Higher-for-Longer World

Bank Indonesia delivered a +25 bps hike on Wednesday (18/11), bringing the BI Rate to 6,00%, with the lending facility at 6,75% and deposit facility at 5,25%. The move split consensus, but the signal is clear: Indonesia is choosing to front-run global risks rather than react to them.

Why now? 
Governor Destry Damayanti framed the hike as pre-emptive — keeping inflation anchored within the 1,5–3,5% YoY target while bracing for a more challenging global backdrop. Senior Deputy Governor Aida Budiman noted the situation has shifted significantly versus last month:
🔹 Persistent geopolitical tensions
🔹 Political instability in Europe
🔹 The AI selloff
🔹 Still-elevated US inflation alongside solid growth

All of which point to a Fed that stays higher-for-longer — and Indonesia is positioning accordingly. The FedWatch Tool now prices a 96,4% probability of a +25 bps Fed hike in December 2026. Since May 2026, BI has now hiked +125 bps cumulatively.

The growth question:
• Cuts to the reserve requirement (GWM)
• Still-loose macroprudential liquidity policy (KLM)
• Solid credit growth with substantial undisbursed loans
Bank Indonesia maintained its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 4,9–5,7%.

Beyond the rate — a stronger stabilization toolkit:
📌 DNDF hedging premium discounts raised from 40% → 45% (6-month tenor) and 45% → 50% (12-month tenor)
📌 A new instrument: Cross Currency Repo (CCR), allowing banks holding USD-denominated securities (SVBI/SUVBI) to obtain rupiah via repo with BI, effective no later than March 2027
📌 Total hedging incentives have driven US$14,1 billion in hedging transactions since June 2026

The rupiah strengthened ~+1% to 18.235, while the IHSG fell -1,07% to 5.247,9 after a positive first session.
This hike reflects a material upgrade in BI's assessment of global macro conditions — the data now strongly signal higher-for-longer, warranting a firmer, measured response. BI's view on a potential December 2026 Fed hike is well-aligned with market pricing.

What to watch going forward:
1️⃣ The Fed's December rate decision
2️⃣ Geopolitical developments and oil prices
3️⃣ Progress on Indonesian capital market reforms, particularly the response to MSCI's downgrade consultation

BI is prioritizing credibility and stability, with a toolkit that goes well beyond the policy rate.

#MoversandShakers
This week, Singapore-based proptech 99 Group is preparing for a leadership transition. Its co-founder is stepping into the chairman’s role, while two senior executives take on expanded responsibilities across Singapore and Indonesia.

✴️ 99 Group names Jason Barakat-Brown as its new Group CEO.
➤ Jason Barakat-Brown will take over as Group CEO on January 1, 2027, succeeding co-founder Darius Cheung, who has led the company for 12 years.

➤ Cheung, who co-founded 99 Group in 2014, will move into the chairman’s role. He will continue shaping the company’s long-term direction.

➤ Barakat-Brown currently serves as Group CFO and CEO of 99 Group Singapore. He joined the company following its acquisition of SRX, where he had been CEO since 2018.

➤ He brings nearly two decades of corporate finance and investment banking experience, including senior leadership roles at UBS, where he headed mergers and acquisitions and corporate finance across Southeast Asia.

➤ His new mandate covers operations across Singapore and Indonesia, with a focus on strategic priorities and financial performance.

➤ Meanwhile, Bharat M. Buxani has taken over as CEO of 99 Group Indonesia, effective October 13, 2026. He will also retain his responsibilities as Group CMO.

➤ Buxani will oversee the Indonesian business, including property platforms Rumah123 and 99.co. His background spans brand positioning, marketing, strategic partnerships and communications.

➤ 99 Group operates several property platforms across both markets, including 99.co, SRX and iProperty.com.sg in Singapore.

➤ The company has confirmed that existing leadership teams, daily operations and client relationships will remain unchanged during the transition.

With two experienced insiders taking on larger operational roles, 99 Group is entering its next phase of leadership while keeping its founder involved in the business.

🗞 More leadership shifts coming next week.

🤯 APAC hiring rules nobody warns you about. #4 will surprise you. 🌏

Hiring across Asia-Pacific? These restrictions catch even seasoned HR teams off guard 👇

🇹🇭 Thailand: the 4-to-1 rule 🧮
A company sponsoring a foreign employee's work permit must show at least 2 million THB in paid-up capital per foreign worker, and keep four Thai employees for every one foreigner.  And that ratio must be maintained continuously, not just at application.  😳

🔓 The loophole: BOI-promoted companies are exempt from the 4:1 ratio and the capital requirement. 

🕵️ Even weirder: one law firm searched hard and found no published legal instrument behind the 4-to-1 ratio.  A rule everyone follows, but few can point to in writing! 👀

⚠️ The penalty is real: an employer who lets a foreigner work outside their permitted scope faces fines of THB 10,000 to 100,000 per worker, and a repeat offence can bring a 3-year ban on employing foreign workers. 

🇮🇩 Indonesia: you must name your replacement 🪪
Indonesia's work permit plan names the worker, position, location and period,  and a named Indonesian counterpart must exist for the role.  Any mismatch between your original application and a renewal means rejection.  😬

🇲🇾 Malaysia: the clock on expats ⏳
Malaysia's EP now starts at RM5,000 a month,  and tenure is capped at 10 years for Categories I and II and 5 years for Category III.  Pass or not, expats have an expiry date! 🗓️

🇵🇭 Philippines: prove no Filipino can do it 📰
The AEP confirms that no Filipino worker is "able, willing, and qualified" to perform the job.  The good news: from 11 Nov 2026, you no longer need to pay for newspaper ads, and processing drops from 15 to 10 business days.  🎉

💡 The pattern: across APAC, the paperwork isn't the hard part. The hidden rules are, like ratios, counterparts and "prove no local can do it" tests.
